text:
I


He Resolves to Return to the Father


Do not fear, Christ the King, if I set out astray

after mad ideals:

neither in my days of tears have I forgotten you,

nor in my hours of happiness have I forgotten you.


In the cruel wound in your side

the soul wishes to form its nest,

forgetting the dreams it has lived

and the sad lies it has dreamed.


In the light of pain, which already shows me

my world of phantoms turned to rubble,

I will go to the foot of your mystical mountain,


with tedium as a staff in my left hand;

with purple rags upon my shoulders,

with a bundle of chimeras on my back.


II


How They Will Rejoice at His Return


I will return like the suffering Prodigal

to your tranquil estate; I can no longer

tend the herd, and I fear

the pitiless brightness of the suns.


You will come out diligently to meet me;

I will tell you quietly, very quietly, of my illness...

and you will leave a kiss upon my brow

and a wedding ring upon my finger;


and gathering around the hearth

the old friends of the neighborhood,

while they eat merrily at your table,


you will cry out in profound rejoicing:

“Rejoice in my happiness, for the son

whom we mourned as lost is returning!”


III


He Weighs the Intensity of the Life to Come


Oh yes, I will return; your love presses

with invincible urgency upon the thought,

which hungers for peace and solitude

in the gentle quiet of the charterhouse.


Oh yes, I will return; already outlined

in the depths of the soul, I sense

the peaceful silhouette of the convent

with its white dome and graceful spire...


There, finally alone with myself,

hearing in Isaiah’s voices

your insinuating cry that calls my name,


how I will drown myself in silence,

how I will lose myself in the cloisters,

how I will merge with the shadow!

translation.title: On the Road
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the three-part devotional sequence, its Prodigal Son imagery, and the return from wandering to a charterhouse.
